item.title: HUD Cuts Off Funding to LA Homelessness Agency in Fraud Settlement
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development announced today that the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority will permanently lose federal funding under a landmark settlement resolving fraud allegations. LAHSA, which has received nearly $1 billion in HUD money over the past five years—more than any other jurisdiction in the nation—will be…
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development announced today that the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority will permanently lose federal funding under a landmark settlement resolving fraud allegations. LAHSA, which has received nearly $1 billion in HUD money over the past five years—more than any other jurisdiction in the nation—will be required to return approximately $150 million and be severed from HUD's homelessness program by the end of 2027.

According to HUD, the agency's Office of Inspector General uncovered evidence of widespread fraud, mismanagement, and oversight failures at LAHSA. Despite receiving the largest share of federal homelessness funding nationwide, Los Angeles has seen homelessness increase and has become what HUD describes as the epicenter of the nation's drug-fueled homelessness crisis. HUD Secretary Marty Turner suspended LAHSA payments in June following the inspector general's findings.

Los Angeles County will assume responsibility for LAHSA's portfolio of projects and programs under strict HUD oversight. The settlement reflects the Trump administration's shift away from the "Housing First" approach toward what it calls "Treatment First" policies focused on addressing addiction and promoting self-sufficiency among unhoused populations.

For Pensacola and the broader Gulf Coast region, the case underscores the federal government's intensified scrutiny of homelessness spending and agencies managing those funds. Local nonprofits and government entities receiving HUD dollars should expect heightened compliance expectations and audit activity.

item.title: UWF celebrates Distinguished Military College designation

item.content:encoded:
The University of West Florida will mark a significant milestone Thursday morning when it formally celebrates its selection as a Distinguished Military College by the U.S. Department of War and its admission into America's Corps of Cadets.

UWF President Manny Diaz Jr., along with Andrew Del Gaudio, executive director of the university's Office of Military Services, and other campus leaders will speak at the 10:30 a.m. event at the Argo Athletic Club on the Pensacola campus. The press conference will outline what the new designation means for UWF's academic mission and military community.

The selection places UWF among a select group of institutions recognized for their commitment to military education and training. The event takes place Thursday, November 19, at 11000 University Parkway.

item.title: Florida Preserves 50,000 Acres of Agricultural Land in Historic Milestone
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Florida's Rural and Family Lands Protection Program has reached a historic milestone, with state officials announcing the preservation of more than 50,000 additional acres of working agricultural land, bringing the total permanently protected through the program to 308,000 acres, according to Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services…
item.content:encoded:
Florida's Rural and Family Lands Protection Program has reached a historic milestone, with state officials announcing the preservation of more than 50,000 additional acres of working agricultural land, bringing the total permanently protected through the program to 308,000 acres, according to Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services Commissioner Wilton Simpson.

The announcement came today as the Governor and Cabinet, acting as the Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund, approved the preservation actions. The easements prevent future development while allowing farms and ranches to continue operating on private land, maintaining agricultural production and contributing to Florida's economy. More than 243,000 of the total preserved acres have been protected during Simpson's tenure as commissioner.

One of the major projects approved is Osceola Prairie, a nearly 19,312-acre cattle and farming operation in Osceola County that will be preserved through a $77.75 million rural lands protection easement. The U.S. Department of Defense is contributing $15 million to the project. The property sits within the Kissimmee River Basin and Northern Everglades ecosystem and includes improved pasture, prairie, scrub, and wetlands, with seven center pivots for crop and hay production serving the cattle operation. It's also adjacent to conservation lands including Kissimmee Prairie Preserve State Park and the Kissimmee River Public Use Area.

All preserved properties are enrolled in the Florida Department of Agriculture's Best Management Practices and are located within the Florida Wildlife Corridor, a priority area established under state law in 2021.

item.title: ECPS Celebrates 34 Students Who Completed State Service Challenge
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Escambia County Public Schools recognized 34 high school students Tuesday for completing the Student Service Challenge, a statewide initiative backed by the Florida Department of Education and Florida Lottery that promotes civic engagement and community service. Participating students from all seven ECPS high schools and Pensacola State College…
item.content:encoded:
Escambia County Public Schools recognized 34 high school students Tuesday for completing the Student Service Challenge, a statewide initiative backed by the Florida Department of Education and Florida Lottery that promotes civic engagement and community service.

Participating students from all seven ECPS high schools and Pensacola State College Charter Academy logged at least 20 hours of volunteer work between September 7 and October 5, volunteering with local organizations and helping people in need. Of the 40 students initially selected to participate, 34 successfully completed the program and submitted written reflections on how their service deepened their understanding of citizenship and leadership.

Each student received a $500 award funded through the Florida Lottery. Laura Touchstone, ECPS Director of High School Education, said the challenge reinforces a key lesson: "These students stepped outside of the classroom, identified needs within their communities, and took action." Superintendent Keith Leonard added that the program reflects the district's commitment to preparing students to be "engaged, compassionate citizens who understand the importance of giving back."

item.content:encoded: Radio and television broadcasts across the country, including in the Pensacola area, will be briefly interrupted today as federal officials conduct a scheduled test of the Emergency Alert System. item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The Emerald Coast Utilities Authority has launched its annual sewer averaging period, which officially kicked off Sunday, November 15. During this time, ECUA uses customer water consumption data from the past 12 months to calculate a more stable sewer charge, rather than billing based on month-to-month fluctuations. For many households and…
item.content:encoded: The Emerald Coast Utilities Authority has launched its annual sewer averaging period, which officially kicked off Sunday, November 15. During this time, ECUA uses customer water consumption data from the past 12 months to calculate a more stable sewer charge, rather than billing based on month-to-month fluctuations. For many households and businesses in the ECUA service area — which covers parts of Escambia and Santa Rosa counties — this averaging approach can provide more predictable billing, especially for those whose water use varies seasonally. The utility typically uses this period to smooth out spikes from summer usage or other temporary consumption patterns, spreading costs more evenly across billing cycles. Customers who have questions about how the averaging period affects their specific accounts can contact ECUA directly for details on their individual calculations.

item.content:encoded:

The bridge opening marks a significant milestone in the ongoing effort to improve traffic flow and safety at one of the region's busiest highway intersections. The project has been designed to address capacity and congestion issues in the area serving commuters and commercial traffic.

This is the first phase of the bridge opening. Additional details about full project completion and the eastern portion timeline were not provided in the initial announcement.

item.content:encoded:
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection is hosting a public meeting today to discuss a draft permit renewal for industrial injection wells at the Ascend Performance Materials facility in Cantonment.

The open house runs from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. at the facility. The meeting gives residents and stakeholders a chance to review the proposed permit and submit comments on the injection well operations.

Ascend Performance Materials, a chemical manufacturer, operates industrial injection wells at its Cantonment location. The permit renewal is part of the state's ongoing environmental oversight of injection well operations in the area.

item.title: Century considers charging youth sports leagues for field use, utilities
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The Town of Century is weighing a new fee structure that would charge youth sports associations for utilities, field use, and other operational costs at town facilities — a move that could effectively shut down youth athletic programs in the community, according to nonprofit sports leaders. Currently, youth sports organizations operate in Century…
item.content:encoded:
The Town of Century is weighing a new fee structure that would charge youth sports associations for utilities, field use, and other operational costs at town facilities — a move that could effectively shut down youth athletic programs in the community, according to nonprofit sports leaders.

Currently, youth sports organizations operate in Century with little to no cost for using municipal fields and facilities. Under the proposed change, the town would begin billing nonprofits for expenses including utilities, maintenance, and supplies like toilet paper.

Youth sports leaders have warned town officials that the fees would be financially prohibitive for volunteer-run organizations and would likely force them to cease operations in Century. The groups say they lack the funding to absorb such costs while still keeping programs affordable and accessible for local families.

The proposal appears to stem from the town's efforts to manage municipal budgets and facility costs. No timeline for a decision has been announced, but the issue is expected to be discussed at upcoming town meetings.

item.title: USPS Reports $6.5B Loss for Fiscal 2026, but Shows Improvement
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The U.S. Postal Service announced Monday that it posted a net loss of $6.5 billion for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2026 — a significant improvement from the prior year's $9.0 billion loss, according to a statement from USPS leadership. The improvement was driven largely by a $2.4 billion increase in operating revenue, which reached $82.9…
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Postal Service announced Monday that it posted a net loss of $6.5 billion for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2026 — a significant improvement from the prior year's $9.0 billion loss, according to a statement from USPS leadership.

The improvement was driven largely by a $2.4 billion increase in operating revenue, which reached $82.9 billion overall — a 3.0 percent jump year-over-year. The agency also benefited from a $2.4 billion decrease in workers' compensation expenses and a $277 million drop in retirement costs. Postmaster General David Steiner credited the revenue gains to strong performance in the USPS Ground Advantage shipping service and the Marketing Mail category, bolstered by price increases in First-Class Mail and Marketing Mail.

However, the Postal Service continues to grapple with systemic financial pressures. Total operating expenses reached $89.4 billion, and the agency's controllable loss — which excludes certain non-manageable costs — stood at $2.4 billion. Steiner said the USPS is balancing daily operations with cash conservation efforts and continues to seek congressional action on legislative reforms to establish a more sustainable business model.

The revenue gains were tempered by declining mail volumes in several categories. First-Class Mail volume fell 5.1 percent while Shipping and Packages volume dropped 5.3 percent, even as the latter category generated stronger revenue through price increases.

District 2 Commissioner-elect Jeff Ates and District 4 Commissioner-elect Dean Light will be sworn in during the ceremony at 6495…
item.content:encoded:
Santa Rosa County will hold an oath of office ceremony Tuesday, November 17 at 2 p.m. at the Administrative Complex in Milton to swear in two newly elected commissioners and reorganize the board for the coming year.

District 2 Commissioner-elect Jeff Ates and District 4 Commissioner-elect Dean Light will be sworn in during the ceremony at 6495 Caroline Street. Following the oath of office, the Board of County Commissioners will convene its annual reorganization meeting to elect a new chairman and vice-chairman.

The ceremony and reorganization meeting will be streamed live and archived online for public viewing. Those needing accommodations under the Americans with Disabilities Act should contact Tom Kristufek, the county's Risk Management Specialist and ADA Coordinator, at 850-983-1838, TTY 711, or ThomasK@santarosa.fl.gov at least 48 hours in advance.

item.title: Florida State Offices to Close Nov. 25, Dec. 23-24, Dec. 31 for Holidays
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Governor Ron DeSantis announced Monday that Florida state offices will shut down on November 25, December 23, December 24, and December 31 to give state employees extended time off during the holiday season. These closures come on top of regularly scheduled state holidays on November 26 and 27 (Thanksgiving week), December 25 (Christmas), and…
item.content:encoded:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced Monday that Florida state offices will shut down on November 25, December 23, December 24, and December 31 to give state employees extended time off during the holiday season.

These closures come on top of regularly scheduled state holidays on November 26 and 27 (Thanksgiving week), December 25 (Christmas), and January 1 (New Year's Day). The combined breaks will give state workers several extended stretches away from the office during the final weeks of the year.

"The First Lady and I want to thank Florida's state employees for their hard work and dedication to serving the people of our state," DeSantis said in a statement. "As we celebrate Thanksgiving and Christmas, we hope they have the opportunity to spend quality time with family and loved ones."

State employees and Florida residents who need services from state agencies should plan accordingly during these closure dates. For specific details about how individual agencies will handle customer service during the holidays, residents can contact their local state office directly.

item.title: ECUA Begins Annual Sewer Averaging Period for Mainland Residents
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: The Emerald Coast Utilities Authority is kicking off its annual sewer averaging period for mainland residential customers, a program that adjusts billing based on consumption patterns over time rather than month-to-month fluctuations. During the averaging period, ECUA calculates sewer charges using a customer's average water consumption rather…
item.content:encoded:
The Emerald Coast Utilities Authority is kicking off its annual sewer averaging period for mainland residential customers, a program that adjusts billing based on consumption patterns over time rather than month-to-month fluctuations.

During the averaging period, ECUA calculates sewer charges using a customer's average water consumption rather than actual monthly usage, which can help smooth out seasonal variations in bills. The program applies to mainland residential customers in Escambia County but does not include Pensacola Beach residents.

Pensacola Beach sewer customers operate under a different billing structure, where charges are based on their actual monthly water consumption rather than the averaging method used elsewhere in the utility's service area.

item.content:encoded: Fairhope residents should expect delays in trash collection this week as the city works through equipment maintenance. According to a city Facebook post, garbage pickup along regular routes was already delayed Monday, November 16, with several trucks currently out for repairs. The City of Fairhope did not provide specifics on how long the repairs might take or which routes would be most affected, but residents in the area should plan accordingly for their trash collection this week.
